sections.title: Follow carbon from air through a food chain
paragraphs: Photosynthesis incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic substances such as glucose. Plants can use this material to build other compounds and tissues. Feeding transfers some of those carbon-containing substances to consumers; neither photosynthesis nor feeding creates carbon atoms.

Aerobic respiration returns carbon dioxide to the surroundings when carbon-containing substrates are broken down. Plants, animals and decomposer organisms respire. A plant can photosynthesise in light and respire at the same time; respiration is not restricted to darkness or animals.

In a cycle diagram, name the substance at each store and the process on each arrow. The arrow from atmospheric carbon dioxide to plant organic material is photosynthesis. The arrow from plant material to an animal is feeding; an arrow from either organism back to carbon dioxide can represent respiration. Energy travels through these processes but is not recycled in the same way as carbon atoms.

example.question: Trace a carbon atom from atmospheric carbon dioxide to a grazing animal and back to the air.
steps: Photosynthesis incorporates the carbon into plant organic material.
The animal eats and assimilates some plant material.
Respiration of a carbon-containing substrate releases carbon dioxide, which can return to the air.
example.explanation: Follow the atom and label each transformation rather than repeating that carbon cycles.

practice.question: Does carbon move directly from atmospheric carbon dioxide into an animal through breathing to build its food?
practice.answer: That is not the food-chain route. An animal obtains organic carbon in its food; the stated pathway begins with photosynthesis by the producer.
practice.explanation: Follow the atom and label each transformation rather than repeating that carbon cycles.

commonMistakes: Do not claim that plants only photosynthesise or that energy is a carbon atom recycled around the diagram.

sections.title: Compare decomposition, storage and combustion
paragraphs: Dead organisms and wastes contain organic carbon. Decomposers break down this material and take up smaller products. Their respiration can return carbon dioxide to the environment. Decomposition does not convert all carbon instantly to gas: some carbon remains in organisms or soil material.

Organic material can be stored for different lengths of time. Fossil-fuel formation involves particular burial and geological conditions over long times; it is not the immediate fate of every dead organism. Combustion of carbon-containing fuels or vegetation releases carbon dioxide when the carbon is fully oxidised. Incomplete burning can also produce carbon monoxide and soot.

An atmospheric carbon budget depends on transfers in both directions. In an original simplified interval, photosynthesis removes 15 arbitrary carbon units while respiration/decomposition return 11 and combustion adds 7. With no other exchanges included, the net change is 11 + 7 − 15 = +3 units. These are invented carbon amounts, not measured atmospheric concentration or energy values.

example.question: In the simplified budget, explain why atmospheric carbon increases although photosynthesis continues.
steps: Return pathways supply 11 + 7 = 18 carbon units.
Photosynthesis removes 15; net gain is 3.
Omitted ocean, soil and transport exchanges limit application to a real atmospheric budget.
example.explanation: Distinguish gross transfers from the net change and describe the model boundary.

practice.question: If combustion in the same model fell from 7 to 4 units, what would the net change be?
practice.answer: 11 + 4 − 15 = 0 units under the stated model; this is a balanced interval, not proof that all carbon movement stops.
practice.explanation: Distinguish gross transfers from the net change and describe the model boundary.

commonMistakes: Do not call all decomposition combustion or infer an actual CO₂ concentration from arbitrary carbon units.

sections.title: Paper 2: make atmospheric nitrogen available
paragraphs: Nitrogen is needed to build amino acids/proteins and nucleic acids. Atmospheric nitrogen gas, N₂, is abundant but ordinary crop plants cannot directly use it in that form. Biological nitrogen fixation converts N₂ into ammonia, which forms ammonium in these biological conditions; it is not simply the absorption of nitrogen gas by a root.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria can live freely or in association with plants. In legume root nodules, bacteria fix nitrogen and supply nitrogen-containing compounds to the plant; the plant supplies organic products of photosynthesis. The bacteria carry out the fixation. A legume without effective nodules does not acquire that ability merely because its roots are present.

Plants can take up nitrate and ammonium and incorporate nitrogen into organic compounds. The school cycle often follows nitrate uptake by roots, protein synthesis, and transfer to an animal through feeding. Keep nitrogen fixation distinct from this uptake/assimilation step. Specific bacterial genus names are not required by this specification.

example.question: Explain how a nodulated legume can acquire nitrogen while a leaf cannot simply build protein from the surrounding N₂.
steps: Associated bacteria convert N₂ into a usable nitrogen form.
Nitrogen-containing products become available to the plant for organic synthesis.
This is a bacterial conversion, not direct plant use of atmospheric nitrogen gas.
example.explanation: Identify the organism and the chemical forms on each side of the process.

practice.question: Is a root absorbing nitrate performing nitrogen fixation?
practice.answer: No. Nitrate uptake uses an already fixed form of nitrogen; fixation changes N₂ into other nitrogen compounds.
practice.explanation: Identify the organism and the chemical forms on each side of the process.

commonMistakes: Do not label plant nitrate uptake or nitrification as conversion of atmospheric N₂.

sections.title: Paper 2: return organic nitrogen to the soil
paragraphs: Proteins and other organic nitrogen compounds in dead organisms and wastes provide material for decomposers. Breakdown can release ammonia/ammonium into the surroundings. This return from organic nitrogen to ammonium is called ammonification; bacteria and fungi can contribute.

Nitrogen does not disappear when an organism dies. Some enters decomposer biomass, some remains in organic material and some returns to inorganic forms. Roots can take up ammonium or nitrate, but the step returning organic material to ammonium is different from the nitrification that can follow.

Connect carbon and nitrogen pathways without confusing their products. Respiration of a carbon-containing substrate can release CO₂, while breakdown of nitrogenous material can release ammonium. Nitrogen gas is not the immediate product of every decomposition step in this school cycle.

example.question: Label the arrow from nitrogen-containing dead leaves and waste to soil ammonium.
steps: Decomposers break down organic nitrogen compounds.
Ammonification returns some nitrogen as ammonia/ammonium.
It is not nitrate-to-N₂ denitrification.
example.explanation: Use named starting and ending forms to make the recycling explanation precise.

practice.question: Does “decomposers recycle nutrients” explain which nitrogen form becomes available?
practice.answer: It is incomplete. State the organic starting material and the ammonia/ammonium returned, then distinguish any later nitrification.
practice.explanation: Use named starting and ending forms to make the recycling explanation precise.

commonMistakes: Do not say that every decomposer immediately converts all waste nitrogen into atmospheric N₂.

sections.title: Paper 2: separate nitrification from fixation
paragraphs: In the usual oxygenated-soil pathway, nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite, and other nitrifying organisms oxidise nitrite to nitrate. The sequence is ammonium → nitrite → nitrate. Nitrification does not start from atmospheric nitrogen gas.

Nitrate can be taken up by roots and used in making organic nitrogen compounds. Nitrification itself is a microbial chemical conversion; assimilation is incorporation into organic material. Nitrification consumes oxygen in this aerobic pathway, so limited soil oxygen can reduce it.

Conditions matter. Waterlogged soil has fewer air-filled spaces and often less oxygen replenishment. A reduced nitrate supply can affect plant growth, but a plant-growth difference alone does not prove nitrification changed: root respiration, soil nutrients and other conditions may also differ.

example.question: A diagram labels ammonium → nitrite → nitrate as nitrogen fixation. Correct it.
steps: The sequence is nitrification.
Nitrifying organisms oxidise the nitrogen forms in oxygenated conditions.
Fixation instead begins with N₂ and produces fixed nitrogen compounds.
example.explanation: Do not infer a uniquely identified microbial pathway from one concentration change.

practice.question: Must falling nitrate in wet soil prove that denitrification is the only process occurring?
practice.answer: No. Uptake, leaching and reduced nitrification can also alter nitrate. Identify the other conditions and transfers before claiming one cause.
practice.explanation: Do not infer a uniquely identified microbial pathway from one concentration change.

commonMistakes: Do not reverse nitrite/nitrate order or confuse atmospheric fixation with ammonium oxidation.

sections.title: Paper 2: return nitrate nitrogen to the atmosphere
paragraphs: Denitrifying bacteria can convert nitrate through intermediate stages to nitrogen gas, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere. This pathway is favoured by low-oxygen conditions with suitable organisms and substrates. It can reduce nitrate available to plants; it is distinct from nitrate uptake and from nitrate carried away in water.

A full school pathway can be followed as N₂ → fixed nitrogen/ammonium → nitrite → nitrate → plant organic nitrogen → animal organic nitrogen → dead material/waste → ammonium. Fixation, nitrification, uptake/assimilation, feeding and decomposition label different arrows. Denitrification is a branch from nitrate towards atmospheric N₂, not a required step between a plant and its consumer.

Real cycles have additional routes and gaseous intermediates, including nitrous oxide in some microbial processes. The simple diagram names the required roles without implying that every nitrate atom follows every arrow, or that all nitrogen loss is harmless N₂. Matter is conserved while its form and location change.

example.question: Explain why a nitrate → N₂ arrow in a low-oxygen soil model points away from the plant-available nitrate store.
steps: Denitrification converts nitrate to gaseous nitrogen forms, represented here by N₂.
This can return nitrogen to the atmosphere and reduce the soil nitrate store.
Leaching would instead move dissolved nitrate to another location without this conversion.
example.explanation: Follow a branch with a named process; the cycle is not one compulsory linear chain.

practice.question: Which pathway converts nitrate into an organic compound in a growing plant?
practice.answer: Uptake followed by assimilation, not denitrification. The destination and chemical form are different.
practice.explanation: Follow a branch with a named process; the cycle is not one compulsory linear chain.

commonMistakes: Do not label nitrate washing out of soil as denitrification or make bacteria create/destroy nitrogen atoms.

sections.title: Explain sulfur dioxide damage through a pathway
paragraphs: Burning sulfur-containing fuel can release sulfur dioxide. Breathing sufficiently polluted air can irritate and harm the respiratory system. High concentrations can also damage plant foliage and reduce growth. State the exposed organism and effect rather than describing all air pollutants as interchangeable.

Sulfur dioxide contributes to reactions producing acidic deposition. Lower pH in susceptible soil or water can disrupt biological processes; nutrient leaching and mobilisation of harmful aluminium can affect roots and aquatic organisms. Sensitivity and soil buffering differ, so the same deposition does not force identical effects at every site.

For an ecological explanation, link the source to the change in conditions and then to organisms or their food supply. Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport by a different mechanism. Neither an acid-rain diagram nor a sulfur dioxide observation alone explains that blood effect.

example.question: Explain a possible route from burning sulfur-containing fuel to fewer acid-sensitive organisms in a poorly buffered lake.
steps: Combustion releases sulfur dioxide.
Atmospheric reactions/deposition can lower lake pH.
Sensitive organisms or their food may be impaired; response depends on buffering and exposure.
example.explanation: Connect pollutant, environmental change and organism response without claiming a universal lethal threshold.

practice.question: Why could two lakes receiving similar acidic deposition respond differently?
practice.answer: Their buffering capacity, chemistry and communities can differ. Deposition amount alone does not specify the biological response.
practice.explanation: Connect pollutant, environmental change and organism response without claiming a universal lethal threshold.

commonMistakes: Do not explain sulfur dioxide solely as a greenhouse gas or use carbon-monoxide haemoglobin binding as its mechanism.

sections.title: Distinguish carbon monoxide from carbon dioxide
paragraphs: Carbon monoxide, CO, can form when carbon-containing material burns incompletely. It is different from carbon dioxide, CO₂. CO binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin and reduces effective oxygen transport to tissues. Its biological consequence is not simply a smaller oxygen percentage in the surrounding air.

Reduced oxygen delivery limits aerobic energy supply to cells, including those in the brain and heart. Effects depend on exposure and vulnerability; severe exposure can be fatal. This is a biological mechanism lesson, not a method for diagnosing poisoning or choosing treatment.

Keep cause and mechanism aligned. Incomplete combustion explains a source of CO; haemoglobin binding explains impaired oxygen delivery. Carbon dioxide’s role in the greenhouse effect and sulfur dioxide’s respiratory/acid-deposition effects should not be substituted for this pathway.

example.question: An explanation says CO harms the body because it creates an acid-rain hole in the lungs. Replace that explanation.
steps: Identify CO as the pollutant from incomplete combustion.
CO binds haemoglobin, reducing effective oxygen transport.
Tissues consequently receive less oxygen for aerobic metabolism.
example.explanation: Name the molecule and its target before explaining the downstream effect.

practice.question: Does writing CO₂ instead of CO preserve the intended blood-transport explanation?
practice.answer: No. They are different molecules with different biological and environmental mechanisms in these syllabus examples.
practice.explanation: Name the molecule and its target before explaining the downstream effect.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse CO with CO₂ or propose deliberate exposure as a practical investigation.

sections.title: Recognise the specified greenhouse gases
paragraphs: The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, methane and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) as greenhouse gases. Write the identities accurately: CO₂ is carbon dioxide, CH₄ methane and N₂O nitrous oxide. N₂ and NO₂ are different substances, not alternate names for N₂O.

These gases interact with outgoing infrared radiation; their effects differ with abundance, lifetime and absorption properties. A list of greenhouse gases is not a ranking of their contributions. CFCs are a family of compounds, not one molecule with a single formula.

Natural greenhouse warming supports Earth’s surface conditions. The enhanced greenhouse effect concerns a change in that radiation balance as greenhouse gas concentrations increase. Ozone depletion concerns a separate atmospheric process, even though CFCs can contribute to both problems.

example.question: Which entries match the named gas list: N₂O, methane, nitrogen gas and water vapour?
steps: N₂O is nitrous oxide; methane and water vapour are also on the specified list.
Nitrogen gas is N₂, not nitrous oxide.
This identification alone does not rank warming contributions.
example.explanation: Distinguish a gas identity from a mechanism and from a contribution ranking.

practice.question: Does describing CFCs only as causing ozone depletion explain their greenhouse role?
practice.answer: No. Their greenhouse role involves infrared absorption; ozone depletion is a different pathway.
practice.explanation: Distinguish a gas identity from a mechanism and from a contribution ranking.

commonMistakes: Do not replace nitrous oxide with nitrogen or nitrogen dioxide, or explain global warming solely through ozone depletion.

sections.title: Link human activities to specific gases
paragraphs: Fossil-fuel combustion transfers stored carbon into atmospheric CO₂. Clearing forests can reduce carbon uptake and release stored carbon through burning or later decomposition. Link the activity to a carbon transfer rather than saying that people manufacture all atmospheric carbon.

Livestock digestion, manure and oxygen-poor organic breakdown in landfills or flooded rice cultivation can contribute methane. Fuel extraction and transport can also leak methane. Agricultural nitrogen additions can increase microbial N₂O production; fertiliser is not itself a gas that must evaporate as nitrous oxide.

CFCs have been used in refrigeration and propellants; release from equipment or other uses adds these industrial compounds to the atmosphere. Do not assume every current refrigerator contains CFCs. This lesson describes the biological/environmental pathway, not current product regulations.

Water vapour commonly acts as a feedback in this explanation: warming supports more atmospheric water vapour, which can amplify greenhouse warming. Distinguish an initiating long-lived-gas increase from that response. It is too simple to describe all the water vapour in air as directly released by factories.

example.question: Give different gas-linked mechanisms for burning coal and adding excess nitrogen fertiliser.
steps: Burning carbon-containing coal releases CO₂.
Added nitrogen can support microbial processes that release N₂O.
The activities and gases differ; name the intermediate process instead of assigning all agriculture only to methane.
example.explanation: Use activity → relevant process → named gas and distinguish emissions from a climatic feedback.

practice.question: Why can warming-related water vapour increase be described as feedback?
practice.answer: The initial warming changes water-vapour conditions; added vapour can strengthen infrared absorption and amplify warming.
practice.explanation: Use activity → relevant process → named gas and distinguish emissions from a climatic feedback.

commonMistakes: Do not claim all gas sources are human, every refrigerator uses CFCs, or fertiliser evaporates unchanged as N₂O.

sections.title: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect
paragraphs: Solar radiation supplies energy to the Earth system. The warmed surface emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared and emit infrared in different directions, including towards the surface. They do not reflect all sunlight back to Earth or prevent all radiation escaping.

Increasing greenhouse gases changes outgoing radiation for the existing temperature profile. More energy can remain in the system until it warms and its energy transfers adjust. At an eventual balance, energy still enters and leaves; a stable temperature does not mean that radiation has stopped.

Global warming means a rise in the long-term global average temperature. Climate change also includes shifts in rainfall, extremes and other conditions. One cold day at one location does not reverse a global long-term warming trend, and this greenhouse explanation is separate from the ozone layer filtering ultraviolet radiation.

example.question: Improve “more greenhouse gas makes a blanket that reflects every ray and permanently stops heat escaping.”
steps: The gases absorb and emit part of Earth’s outgoing infrared.
An increase alters the energy balance at the former temperature and can cause warming.
Energy continues to escape; the effect is not total blockage or reflection of all incident sunlight.
example.explanation: State radiation type, gas action and the change in balance before describing temperature.

practice.question: Would an energy balance after warming mean the atmosphere contains no greenhouse gases?
practice.answer: No. Ongoing incoming/outgoing transfers can balance at a warmer state while greenhouse absorption/emission continues.
practice.explanation: State radiation type, gas action and the change in balance before describing temperature.

commonMistakes: Do not substitute ozone holes, reflected visible sunlight or no escaping energy for the greenhouse mechanism.

sections.title: Explain consequences without predicting every place alike
paragraphs: Changing temperature and rainfall can alter water supply, growing conditions, habitats and the distribution or timing of organisms. A shifted flowering season may affect its relationship with pollinators. Whether a species can persist also depends on its tolerances, movement and the availability of suitable habitat.

Sea level can rise when land ice adds water to oceans and when seawater expands as it warms. This can affect coastal habitats, flooding and saline intrusion. Melting ice that is already floating is a different case; it is not the same direct addition of new ocean water from land.

Rainfall changes are uneven: some regions can face greater drought risk while others experience heavier rainfall and flooding. Crop responses depend on water, heat, pests and adaptation, not temperature alone. Distinguish a plausible causal consequence from a guaranteed numerical forecast; none of the scenarios here is a site-specific prediction.

example.question: Explain two pathways by which warming can threaten a coastal ecosystem and a water-limited crop.
steps: Land-ice melt/thermal expansion can raise sea level and change coastal inundation or salinity.
Changed heat and rainfall can reduce available water or increase stress for the crop.
Actual effects depend on the local exposure, species and management.
example.explanation: Connect a physical change to a biological response and state the relevant conditions.

practice.question: Does a longer growing season guarantee that crop yield increases everywhere?
practice.answer: No. Water shortage, damaging heat, pests and other constraints can outweigh the extra growing time.
practice.explanation: Connect a physical change to a biological response and state the relevant conditions.

commonMistakes: Do not claim identical rainfall/yield effects everywhere or attribute the same sea-level mechanism to floating and land ice.

sections.title: Explain how sewage can lower dissolved oxygen
paragraphs: Untreated or inadequately treated sewage can add organic material, nutrients and harmful microorganisms to water. These are different routes of harm. Organic material supplies substrates to decomposers; nutrients can also stimulate aquatic growth. A water sample’s appearance alone does not establish whether it is safe or identify a cause.

Aerobic microorganisms breaking down added organic matter respire and consume dissolved oxygen. If oxygen demand exceeds replacement by aeration and photosynthesis, oxygen concentration falls. Sensitive aquatic organisms may be stressed, move away or die; not every organism has the same tolerance.

A high biochemical oxygen demand describes oxygen use during specified conditions/time, not oxygen already dissolved in the river. Oxygen depletion is separate from infection by pathogens. Decomposition can continue through anaerobic routes in low-oxygen zones, so do not claim all microbial activity instantly stops when oxygen falls.

example.question: Explain a possible fall in dissolved oxygen after a discharge rich in organic sewage material.
steps: Organic substrates support microbial activity.
Aerobic respiration consumes dissolved oxygen.
Where demand exceeds replenishment, less oxygen remains for sensitive aquatic organisms.
example.explanation: State substrate → aerobic respiration → oxygen balance → biological consequence.

practice.question: Does a low dissolved-oxygen reading prove that sewage is the only cause?
practice.answer: No. Temperature, flow, algal respiration, other organic inputs and measurement timing can also matter. Compare source and environmental evidence.
practice.explanation: State substrate → aerobic respiration → oxygen balance → biological consequence.

commonMistakes: Do not equate biochemical oxygen demand with oxygen concentration or treat pathogens and oxygen depletion as the same mechanism.

sections.title: Follow fertiliser pollution through eutrophication
paragraphs: Mineral nutrients not taken up by crops can be transported from land to water. Leaching carries dissolved substances through soil; runoff carries water and dissolved or suspended material over the surface. Excess nitrate or phosphate reaching water can remove a nutrient limitation and support excessive algal growth.

Dense growth can reduce light reaching submerged plants. If plants or algae die, decomposers use the organic material; aerobic respiration consumes dissolved oxygen. Oxygen-demanding decomposition and community respiration can then exceed oxygen supply, harming sensitive aquatic life.

Mineral nutrients do not directly consume oxygen merely by being fertiliser, and algae can produce oxygen during photosynthesis. Nutrient enrichment is the initiating input; reduced light, biomass turnover and respiration explain the later oxygen problem. Not every bloom is toxic and not every enriched water body immediately loses all oxygen.

example.question: Order the causal links from excess field nutrients to oxygen stress in a simplified lake scenario.
steps: Nutrients are transported to the water and support algal growth.
Dense growth shades submerged plants; dead organic material increases.
Aerobic decomposition/respiration raises oxygen demand.
Dissolved oxygen can fall when consumption exceeds replenishment, affecting sensitive organisms.
example.explanation: Link each stage to the next and separate the nutrient input from the oxygen-consuming process.

practice.question: What is missing from “fertiliser enters a lake and takes away oxygen”?
practice.answer: Explain the biological intermediates: nutrient-supported growth, organic matter and oxygen-consuming respiration. The mineral input itself is not the complete mechanism.
practice.explanation: Link each stage to the next and separate the nutrient input from the oxygen-consuming process.

commonMistakes: Do not say every bloom makes toxins or that photosynthesis by algae always consumes oxygen.

diagram.alt: Original six-stage conditional pathway: nutrients enter water, excess algal growth, less light/dead biomass, aerobic decomposition, oxygen demand can exceed supply, sensitive aquatic organisms harmed.
diagram.caption: A simplified nutrient-to-oxygen pathway. Daytime photosynthesis can add oxygen; the balance changes with time and conditions.

sections.title: Interpret oxygen data with time and conditions
paragraphs: Photosynthetic organisms release oxygen in light while organisms also respire. At night photosynthetic oxygen production stops, but respiration continues. A nutrient-enriched site can therefore have a high afternoon reading and a low predawn reading; one daytime value does not establish adequate oxygen throughout the day.

Original invented readings for the same depths/sites are A: afternoon 10 mg/L and predawn 3 mg/L; comparison B: 8 mg/L and 6 mg/L. The two reading differences are 7 mg/L and 2 mg/L. They are differences between observations, not respiration rates, and do not show an organism-specific lethal threshold.

To investigate the explanation, take repeated time-matched readings and record depth, temperature, light, flow and nutrient/organic inputs. A pair of observations cannot identify which source caused the pattern. Oxygen also exchanges with the air and can be redistributed by mixing.

example.question: Why does the invented afternoon value of 10 mg/L at A not rule out oxygen stress?
steps: Its predawn value is much lower at 3 mg/L.
Production and consumption change through the day, so one high value misses the low period.
The data do not alone establish a cause, a respiration rate or a lethal threshold.
example.explanation: Describe what the data show before choosing a mechanism, and identify missing controls/intervals.

practice.question: Can you calculate a net oxygen-consumption rate per hour from just these unlabeled-time pairs?
practice.answer: No. Exact time intervals and other oxygen transfers are missing; the concentration differences alone are not a microbial respiration rate.
practice.explanation: Describe what the data show before choosing a mechanism, and identify missing controls/intervals.

commonMistakes: Do not infer constant oxygen from an afternoon reading or calculate a process rate without time and balance information.

sections.title: Paper 2: separate mineral leaching from soil erosion
paragraphs: Removing trees can reduce root binding, canopy interception and protective vegetation/litter cover. Rain and surface runoff can then detach and carry soil more readily, particularly where replacement cover is poor. Soil erosion moves particles; it is not simply a dissolved nutrient changing position.

Leaching removes dissolved minerals with water moving through soil. Reduced uptake and changed drainage after clearance can increase mineral losses under suitable conditions. Loss of nutrient-rich topsoil through erosion also reduces fertility, but the transport mechanism differs from dissolved leaching.

Effects depend on slope, soil, rainfall and management after clearance. Comparing an exposed steep site with a covered flat one changes more than tree cover. Loss of habitats and altered microclimate can also affect organisms; avoid claiming a single identical erosion rate or biodiversity outcome for every cleared site.

example.question: Classify dissolved nitrate moving down through soil and muddy particles leaving in overland water after clearance.
steps: Dissolved nitrate moving through soil is leaching.
Detached soil particles transported away are erosion.
Both can lower soil fertility through different routes.
example.explanation: Name what moves and how it moves, then explain the biological effect and comparison limits.

practice.question: Why does matching slope matter in a tree-cover comparison?
practice.answer: Slope changes runoff and erosion independently of cover; unequal slopes confound the comparison.
practice.explanation: Name what moves and how it moves, then explain the biological effect and comparison limits.

commonMistakes: Do not describe all soil loss as leaching or treat different sites as a controlled tree-removal experiment.

sections.title: Paper 2: connect clearance to carbon, gases and water
paragraphs: Removing photosynthesising trees reduces that vegetation’s CO₂ uptake. Burning cleared biomass or later respiration during decomposition can release stored carbon as CO₂. The net result also depends on regrowth, replacement vegetation and other transfers, so a removed carbon store is not necessarily all released immediately.

Photosynthesis takes up CO₂ and releases O₂; aerobic respiration and combustion use O₂ and can release CO₂. Clearance changes these linked fluxes. This does not mean local tree loss makes atmospheric oxygen instantly disappear: the atmosphere has large stores and many interacting sources/sinks.

Evapotranspiration combines evaporation from surfaces with transpiration by plants. Fewer trees can reduce the transpiration component and alter humidity, rainfall recycling and local water movement. Direction and scale depend on replacement cover and conditions; soil evaporation can change too. “No trees means no rain anywhere” is not a valid water-cycle explanation.

example.question: Explain a carbon route and a water-cycle route affected by removal of a woodland.
steps: Reduced tree photosynthesis can lower CO₂ uptake; burning/decay can return stored carbon.
Reduced tree transpiration can reduce water-vapour return and alter local/regional water processes.
Specify replacement cover and conditions; neither carbon release nor loss of all rain is instantaneous or universal.
example.explanation: Connect vegetation change to named fluxes rather than treating gas/water stores as vanishing.

practice.question: Does a reduction in tree transpiration prove every component of evaporation has ceased?
practice.answer: No. Water can still evaporate from soil and other surfaces; evapotranspiration has more than one component.
practice.explanation: Connect vegetation change to named fluxes rather than treating gas/water stores as vanishing.

commonMistakes: Do not say trees create carbon, clearance instantly removes atmospheric oxygen, or reduced transpiration means no evaporation.
